title: Cello Concerto in E minor
hook: Elgar’s last major work, written in the year after the First World War; quiet, autumnal and deeply private.

painting.title: We Are Making a New World
painting.pairingNote: A pale sun over a shattered wood on the Western Front, painted the year before the concerto; Elgar’s music, written in the months after the war, mourns a lost world in a much quieter voice.

facts: In 1918, the night after he came home from hospital, Elgar wrote down the melody that became the concerto’s main theme. He finished the work in 1919 at Brinkwells, a cottage in the Sussex woods, after three chamber works written there.

The first performance, on 27 October 1919 with Felix Salmond and the London Symphony Orchestra, was a disaster: another conductor used up most of the rehearsal time. The critic Ernest Newman still called the music “lovely stuff, very simple”.
It is Elgar’s last major work. His wife Alice died in April 1920, and he never finished another large-scale piece.
The concerto became famous only in the 1960s, through this recording by Jacqueline du Pré, then aged 20.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a proud cello recitative and a sad, swaying song (I), a flickering, nervous [[scherzo|scherzo]] (II), a short, slow lament (III), a striding finale that looks back before it ends (IV).

movements.heading: Adagio – Moderato
movements.summary: The cello begins alone with loud, solemn chords, like a speech. Then the violas, on their own, introduce a sad, swaying melody that the cello takes over. A lighter middle section in E major brings brief relief before the melody returns, and the movement leads straight into the next.

mainIdeas.name: The opening chords
mainIdeas.description: a short, proud [[recitative|recitative]] for the cello, marked *nobilmente* (“nobly”).

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: a sad, swaying melody in 9/8, first on the violas.

stops.hear: The cello alone plays loud, rich chords; clarinets, bassoons and a horn answer briefly
The cello runs freely up and down, then sinks to its lowest notes
The violas alone, quietly, play a sad, swaying melody
The cello takes the melody over
The strings play the theme again and the cello answers with a loud, anguished outburst
The music turns lighter and warmer; a lilting melody in E major
The swaying melody returns

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The melody fades away, and without a pause the music moves into the next movement

notice: Listen for who plays the main theme first. It is not the soloist but the violas, alone, before the cello takes over.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Jacqueline du Pré was 20 when she recorded the concerto with John Barbirolli and the London Symphony Orchestra at Kingsway Hall on 19 August 1965. The story goes that during a break she left the hall and came back to find an audience of local musicians and critics who had heard that something special was happening. On the Spotify album the concerto is tracks 1–4, followed by *Sea Pictures* with Janet Baker.

movements.heading: Lento – Allegro molto
movements.summary: After some hesitant starts, plucked chords and short bursts of speed, the cello sets off on a very fast, very light perpetual motion. It is a flickering [[scherzo|scherzo]] that never settles, with the orchestra adding quick comments.

mainIdeas.name: The flicker
mainIdeas.description: rapid repeated notes on the cello, very quiet and light.

stops.hear: The cello plays plucked chords, then tries a fast figure and stops, more than once
stops.happening: The slow, hesitant opening, with [[pizzicato|pizzicato]] chords

stops.hear: A brief free passage for the cello alone
The cello takes off in very fast, light repeated notes
The fast figure keeps running; the orchestra adds quick, sharp comments

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A quick rush to a short, crisp ending

notice: Notice how quietly the fast music is played. It is a whisper at high speed, not a display of power.

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: A short slow movement and the heart of the concerto: a single melody for the cello, sung almost without a break over a soft orchestra. One theme runs through the whole movement.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a long, tender melody that rises and falls in short phrases.

stops.hear: The cello sings a slow, tender melody over a soft accompaniment
The melody climbs higher and grows more intense
The line reaches its warmest, fullest point, then begins to fall

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The melody fades and the movement ends quietly

notice: Follow the cello from start to finish. It hardly ever stops singing, and the orchestra stays almost entirely in the background.

movements.heading: Allegro – Moderato – Allegro, ma non troppo – Poco più lento – Adagio
movements.tempo: Allegro – Moderato – Allegro, ma non troppo – Poco più lento – Adagio
movements.summary: The longest movement. After a short, loud start and another recitative, the cello launches a striding, proud theme. Near the end the music slows, a new aching theme appears, the slow movement’s melody returns, and the cello’s opening chords come back before a brief, abrupt ending.

mainIdeas.name: The striding theme
mainIdeas.description: a bold, march-like tune marked *risoluto*, with sudden changes of key.

mainIdeas.name: The memories
mainIdeas.description: the Adagio’s melody and the opening recitative, recalled near the end.

stops.hear: The orchestra rises quickly to a loud outburst
The cello alone, speaking freely again
The cello strikes up a bold, striding tune
stops.happening: The main theme, *Allegro, ma non troppo*

stops.hear: The tune moves through many keys; the cello has quick, agile passages
stops.happening: Episodes, always returning to the striding theme

stops.hear: The striding tune returns in the orchestra and cello
The music slows; a new, aching theme appears, with heavy accents
Slower still; the melody of the third movement returns, and the orchestra holds a long chord
The cello plays the loud opening chords of the first movement

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The striding theme rushes back; three short chords end the concerto

notice: When the cello’s opening chords return near the end, compare them with the very first seconds of the concerto. The circle closes.
Notice how short the final fast section is. After the long farewell, Elgar ends in a few seconds.

threads.title: After the war
threads.body: Written in 1918–19, the concerto is contemplative and elegiac rather than heroic, very different from Elgar’s earlier, grander music.

threads.title: A recitative that returns
threads.body: The cello’s opening chords frame the whole work and come back just before the end.

threads.title: The cello as speaker
threads.body: Free, speech-like passages appear in three of the four movements.

threads.title: Rediscovered
threads.body: Neglected for decades, the concerto became one of the two most performed cello concertos, with Dvořák’s, after du Pré’s recording.

recordings.label: His Master's Voice (EMI); now Warner Classics
